claims.text: Microstructural heterogeneity in a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy causes localized electrochemical potential differences at phase interfaces.
Electrochemical potential differences at phase interfaces lead to preferential interfacial corrosion.
Preferential interfacial corrosion locally weakens the alloy.
Corrosion-induced local weakening accelerates mechanical wear.
The interaction between interfacial corrosion and wear produces synergistic accelerated degradation.
The interfacial regions between eutectic phases have compositional differences.
The interfacial regions between eutectic phases have electrochemical potential differences.
Localized galvanic coupling between distinct eutectic phases induces selective corrosion at their interfaces.
Degradation of the interfacial regions reduces mechanical integrity.
The total degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion will exceed the sum of degradation from wear and corrosion acting individually.
The eutectic microstructure will exhibit more severe localized interfacial corrosion than a homogenized baseline alloy.
The eutectic microstructure will exhibit greater wear than a homogenized baseline alloy.
Homogenization reduces strong interfacial electrochemical disparities.
The proposed effect requires temperature and environmental conditions that promote active corrosion kinetics.
The proposed effect requires mechanical loading sufficient to exploit corrosion-weakened interfacial regions.
The synergistic effect may not be apparent at lower temperatures or in less aggressive environments.
The magnitude of the interfacial galvanic effect depends on compositional gradients and microstructural details.
